g:IT/piemonte.title: Piemonte
g:IT/piemonte.atlas_note: Piemonte grows wine on hills, not plains. South of the Po the Langhe, Roero and Monferrato are young marine sediments of marl and sand, while the north rests on the roots of a Permian supervolcano and on glacial moraines. The climate is temperate with cold winters, shaped by the Alps on three sides and by sea air from Liguria to the south. Barolo and Barbaresco were among the first DOC in 1966, and the vineyard landscape of Langhe-Roero and Monferrato became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2014.
geology: The wine hills south of the Po (Langhe, Roero, Monferrato, Gavi, Tortona) are marine sediments of the Tertiary Piedmont Basin, Oligocene to Pliocene in age. The northern hills (Alto Piemonte) sit on the roots of a Permian supervolcano and on Pleistocene glacial moraines, and the Canavese lies inside the Ivrea morainic amphitheatre.
Tertiary sedimentary rocks of the Langhe-Roero and Monferrato hills (Tertiary)
ICOMOS describes the soil of the UNESCO property as mainly sedimentary rock of the Tertiary period, low in organic matter and rich in mineral elements.
Bacino Terziario del Piemonte (Tertiary Piedmont Basin) (Tertiary)
Named in the Colli Tortonesi disciplinare (art. 9) as the stratigraphic succession under the Tortona hills.
Langhe marine succession (Miocene, about 12 to 5 Ma)
The Consorzio of the Langhe says its sediments formed on a sea floor about 12 to 5 million years ago.
Sesia supervolcano (Permian, about 290 to 280 Ma)
Magmatic system active between 290 and 280 Ma, main eruption about 280 Ma, caldera at least 13 km across, between Valsesia, Valsessera and Lake Maggiore.
Anfiteatro Morenico di Ivrea (Pleistocene, about 900,000 to 11,500 years BP)
505 km2 of moraines left by the Dora Baltea glacier in about ten glaciations.
climate: Temperate. The Barolo area is classed Koppen Cfa (warm temperate, humid, hot summer).
14.3 °C mean, 898 mm rain a year. Urban station, warmer than the wine hills.
The Alps close the region to the north and west; the Langhe consorzio names the Alps and mild humid currents from the Ligurian Sea as the main influences.
Sea air crosses the low Ligurian Apennines to the southern hills. The Grignolino del Monferrato Casalese disciplinare puts the Alps about 130 km and the sea about 90 km from Casale.
Warm, humid air rises from the Tanaro valley into the Barolo hills.
g:IT/piemonte.altitude_text: Range set by the disciplinari quoted for the areas: lowest 120 m (Grignolino del Monferrato Casalese, art. 8), highest 700 m (Carema, art. 9; art. 4 allows 300 to 600 m). Most hill vineyards lie between about 150 and 550 m.
history: 5th century BC
Vine pollen from the 5th century BC has been found in the area of the UNESCO property.
mid-18th century
Barolo was exported in bottle at least from the mid-18th century.
mid-19th century
Giulia Colbert Falletti, last Marchesa di Barolo, and Cavour helped set up the making of Barolo (Barolo disciplinare art. 10).
The Champagne method was applied to Moscato in Asti and Canelli.
The government founded the Regia Stazione Enologica Sperimentale in Gattinara (Gattinara disciplinare art. 9).
Barolo and Barbaresco became DOC by DPR of 23 April 1966, among the first Italian denominations.
Barolo became DOCG by DPR of 1 July 1980 and Barbaresco by DPR of 3 October 1980.
On 22 June 2014 the World Heritage Committee in Doha inscribed the Vineyard Landscape of Piedmont: Langhe-Roero and Monferrato.
grapes: 44,471 ha. Vineyard area (superficie vitata) of Piemonte for 2024, 44,471 ha, in the official series published by Regione Piemonte and Vignaioli Piemontesi in L'Annata Vitivinicola in Piemonte 2025 (Dec 2025): 2016 43,500; 2017 44,202; 2018 44,449; 2019 44,677; 2020 44,737; 2021 45,420; 2022 45,823 (peak); 2023 44,285; 2024 44,471; 2025 43,792 (estimate, final figure due January 2026). The 2024 figure was first given as provisional in January 2025 and is unchanged in the December 2025 series. Other measures for 2024: 43,670 ha suitable for DO wine and 36,193 ha claimed for DO wine at the 2024 harvest (Regione Piemonte, Qualche dato sul vino piemontese oggi); 39,400 ha in the ISTAT crop statistics; about 46,000 ha in AGEA data for 2025 (I numeri del vino).

Barbera 24.2%, Moscato Bianco 23.6%, Nebbiolo 16.4%, Dolcetto 7.5%, Cortese 6.4%, Arneis 3.2%, Chardonnay 3.1%, Pinot Nero 1.8%. Both put Barbera and Moscato Bianco near 24% each and Nebbiolo near 16 to 17%.
Most planted grape of Piemonte: 10,099 ha of 41,699 ha in the 2024 regional vineyard register. (secondary source)

g:IT/toscana.title: Toscana
g:IT/toscana.atlas_note: Tuscany grows wine from the Apennine foothills to the Tyrrhenian coast. The Chianti hills are old sandstone, limestone and shale; the hills of Siena and San Gimignano are Pliocene sea floor; the coast has young gravels and sands. The climate turns from continental inland to Mediterranean by the sea, with rain falling from about 900 mm in Chianti to about 600 mm at Bolgheri. Sangiovese covers 57% of the vineyard, and the 1716 Medici edict was one of the first legal delimitations of wine zones.
geology: Inland Tuscany is Apennine rock: Oligocene macigno sandstone and Cretaceous to Eocene flysch with alberese limestone and galestro shale in the Chianti hills. South and west of them lie Pliocene marine sands and clays (Siena, Montepulciano, San Gimignano). The coast has Pleistocene conglomerates and sands (Bolgheri).
Macigno del Chianti (Oligocene)
Feldspathic sandstone of the Chianti anticline, on low mountains and high hills.
Alberese in clay-marl flysch (Cretaceous)
Marly limestone within a Cretaceous clay-marl flysch.
Pliocene marine sands and clays (Pliocene)
Base of Montepulciano (art. 9) and San Gimignano (art. 9).
Conglomerati di Bolgheri (Middle Pleistocene)
Coastal conglomerates named by Mazzanti (1983).
climate: Mediterranean on the coast and in the south, more continental in the inland hills.
15.7 °C mean, 791 mm rain a year. Rain series accepts up to three missing days a month.
The Apennines form the north-eastern ridge that shelters Chianti from the Po valley. (secondary source)
Sea breezes cool the Bolgheri coast; Montalcino is 40 km from the sea.
Rainfall falls from 800 to 900 mm in Chianti Classico (art. 9) to about 584 mm at Bolgheri (art. 9) and 620 mm at Scansano (art. 10).
g:IT/toscana.altitude_text: From 10 m on the Bolgheri coast (Consorzio) to 700 m in Chianti Classico (art. 4 limit) and 750 m at Pomino (art. 9).
history: Vernaccia is recorded in the Ordinamenti delle Gabelle of San Gimignano (art. 9).
First notarial deed naming Chianti wine (Chianti Classico art. 9).
Francesco Redi's 'Bacco in Toscana' praises Montepulciano wine (Vino Nobile art. 9).
Grand Duke Cosimo III de' Medici defined the boundaries of Chianti, Pomino, Carmignano and Val d'Arno di Sopra; the bando of 24 September 1716 barred the names outside those areas. (secondary source)
DM of 31 July 1932 delimited Chianti and its zones, and allowed 'Classico' for the historic zone.
Vernaccia di San Gimignano became the first Italian DOC on 3 March 1966; Brunello di Montalcino followed by DPR of 28 March 1966.
Brunello di Montalcino and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano became DOCG by DPR of 1 July 1980; the Brunello consorzio calls Brunello the first wine to become DOCG.
Chianti Classico got its own disciplinare, separate from Chianti, by decree of 5 August 1996.
grapes: 61,430.8 ha. Planted vineyard area in the ARTEA schedario viticolo at 31 July 2024 (Regione Toscana, presentation of 3 Feb 2025). Of this, 58,079 ha (94.5%) is eligible for DOCG or DOC. ISMEA-based press material gave almost 61,000 ha in Feb 2024.

Sangiovese 57.2%, Merlot 8.1%, Cabernet Sauvignon 5.9%, Trebbiano Toscano 3.5%, Vermentino 3.5%, Cabernet Franc 2.3%, Syrah 2.3%, Chardonnay 1.3%. g:IT/piemonte/langhe-and-roero.title: Langhe
g:IT/piemonte/langhe-and-roero.atlas_note: The Langhe are the hills south of the Tanaro around Alba. Their soils are Miocene sea floor: grey marls and sands laid down about 12 to 5 million years ago and now tilted, so the Barolo zone has older Serravallian rocks to the east and younger Tortonian marls to the west. The climate is temperate with cold winters, warmed by air from the Tanaro and cooled toward the Alps in the south. Barolo and Barbaresco, both 100% Nebbiolo, were DOC in 1966 and DOCG in 1980.
geology: Miocene marine marls and sands of the Tertiary Piedmont Basin, tilted so that older layers crop out to the south east and younger ones to the north west. In Barolo the older Serravallian formations (Lequio, Diano sandstone) form the eastern side (Serralunga d'Alba, Monforte d'Alba, part of Castiglione Falletto); the younger Tortonian Marne di Sant'Agata Fossili form the western side (La Morra, Verduno, Barolo).
Formazione di Murazzano (Langhian to Serravallian (15.9 to 11.6 Ma))
Calcareous marls with thin fine sand layers; only at the highest elevations south of Clavesana and Belvedere Langhe.
Formazione di Lequio (Serravallian (13.8 to 11.6 Ma))
Alternating marly clay and sand, very calcareous soils; in the Barolo, Barbaresco and Dogliani areas.
Arenarie di Diano d'Alba (Tortonian (11.6 to 7.2 Ma))
Sandy layers from submarine landslides; sandier, less calcareous soils in Monforte d'Alba, Castiglione Falletto, Barolo and Diano d'Alba.
Marne di Sant'Agata Fossili (Tortonian to Messinian (11.6 to 5.3 Ma))

The most widespread formation of the Barolo and Barbaresco Langa, mainly marl with little sand. A study of Barolo vineyards on these grey marls found alkaline soils (pH 7.8 to 8.7) with 21.7% calcium carbonate on average.
Conglomerati di La Morra (Messinian (7.2 to 5.3 Ma))
Thick pebbly layers, only in La Morra, giving gravelly soils.
Formazione Gessoso-Solfifera (Messinian)
Clay marls with large gypsum crystals, on the west-facing slope of the La Morra and Verduno hill.
Formazione di Cassano Spinola (Messinian)
A sandy and a marly part, between La Morra and Verduno.
Tortonian marls and thin sands (legal wording) (Tortonian)
The Barolo (art. 10) and Barbaresco (art. 9) disciplinari both describe the soils as 'terreno tortoniano' of marls and thinly layered sands.
Tortonian / Serravallian divide in Barolo (Tortonian younger, Serravallian (once called Helvetian) older)
Western communes (La Morra, Verduno) mainly Tortonian; eastern Serralunga d'Alba and Monforte d'Alba mainly Serravallian; the Cannubi hill in Barolo has both. (secondary source)
climate: Cold subcontinental temperate according to the Consorzio; Koppen Cfa at Barolo according to the University of Turin study.

Five Regione Piemonte agrometeorological stations in the Barolo zone (Serralunga Boscareto 405 m, Barolo 360 m, La Morra 326 m, Castiglione Falletto 309 m, Serralunga Fontanafredda 309 m) · 14 to 20 years per station, starting 1999 to 2005 and ending 2018
13.3 °C mean, 800 mm rain a year. Temperature range between years 12 to 14.2 C; rainfall 488 to 1250 mm. Peer reviewed study, University of Turin.
The Alps and mild humid currents from the Ligurian Sea shape the climate.

Barolo has intermediate temperatures and shelter from wind, with warm humid air rising from the Tanaro valley. Barbaresco, lower and nearer the river, is milder and drier than the other zones. Dogliani, nearer the Alps, is the coolest.
Novello is one of the coolest Barolo communes because of winds from the Cottian Alps. (secondary source)
g:IT/piemonte/langhe-and-roero.altitude_text: Barolo vineyards must lie between 170 and 540 m (art. 4); Barbaresco vineyards no higher than 550 m (art. 4). Some La Morra vineyards are above 1,400 ft (about 430 m).
history: mid-18th century
Barolo exported in bottle at least from the mid-18th century.
mid-19th century
The castle of Grinzane and its estate belonged to the Count of Cavour; Giulia Colbert Falletti and Cavour helped establish Barolo.
Barolo and Barbaresco DOC by DPR of 23 April 1966. The Barbaresco disciplinare calls it one of the first denominations recognised in Italy, together with Barolo.
Barolo DOCG by DPR of 1 July 1980; Barbaresco DOCG by DPR of 3 October 1980.
Three of the six UNESCO components are in the Langhe: Langa of Barolo (core 3,051 ha), Grinzane Cavour Castle (7 ha) and Hills of Barbaresco (891 ha).
grapes: Dogliani DOCG is 100% Dolcetto (secondary); the Consorzio calls the Dogliani zone the coolest of the Langhe (official). (secondary source)
Piemonte's most planted grape; in the Langhe it makes Barbera d'Alba. (secondary source)
study_points: Barolo vineyards: 170 to 540 m, and new plantings exclude north-facing slopes from -45 to +45 degrees (art. 4).
Barbaresco vineyards: no higher than 550 m, north-facing slope excluded (art. 4).
Marne di Sant'Agata Fossili (Tortonian to Messinian) is the most common formation in the Barolo and Barbaresco Langa.
Serralunga d'Alba and Monforte d'Alba sit mostly on older Serravallian soils; La Morra and Verduno on younger Tortonian soils. (secondary source)
The Barolo zone averages about 13.3 C and 800 mm a year (Regione Piemonte agrometeorological stations, about 2000 to 2018).

g:IT/piemonte/langhe-and-roero.title: Roero
g:IT/piemonte/langhe-and-roero.atlas_note: The Roero lies north of Alba on the left bank of the Tanaro. Its hills are Pliocene sands and clays, younger and looser than the Langhe marls, cut by the steep Rocche where the old Tanaro was diverted. Sandy soils suit the white Arneis, which is grown here since the 1400s, and give a lighter, more perfumed Nebbiolo. The Roero was DOC in 1985 and DOCG in 2004.
geology: Pliocene marine and coastal sands and clays on the left bank of the Tanaro, younger and sandier than the Langhe. When the Tanaro was diverted east in the Pleistocene, regressive erosion cut the steep scarps called the Rocche.
Sabbie di Asti (Astian yellow sands) (Pliocene, about 5 to 3.5 Ma (beach deposits))
Loose yellow sands that form most of the Roero hills.
Argille di Lugagnano (Pliocene (Piacenzian))
Grey-blue marine marls rich in fossils, impermeable, under the sands in the southern Roero valleys. (secondary source)
Unita di Ferrere (Pliocene, about 3.5 to 2.5 Ma (delta deposits))
Delta deposits above the Asti sands.
Villafranchian deposits and red loess (Pliocene to early Pleistocene)
Marly, gravelly and pebbly deposits cover large areas of the plateau, with bright red loess. (secondary source)
Rocche del Roero (Pleistocene erosion)

Steep scarps left by regressive erosion after the capture of the Tanaro. At Pocapaglia the scarp is about 100 m high and 30 km long. The Roero disciplinare (art. 9) links the layered sands, clays and limestone of the zone to the 'cattura del Tanaro'.
climate: Temperate, as in the Langhe; no official station normals were found for the Roero.
The Roero disciplinare (art. 9) cites day-night temperature swings as a factor in the acidity of the sparkling Arneis.
history: 15th century
Arneis has been grown in the Roero since the 1400s, when it was known by a name referring to the 'bric Renesio' (art. 9).
Roero DOC by DPR of 18 March 1985.
Roero DOCG by DM of 7 December 2004.
grapes: Roero Arneis: at least 95% Arneis (art. 2); Arneis vineyards may also face north (art. 4).
Roero (red) and Roero Riserva: at least 95% Nebbiolo (art. 2).
study_points: Roero soils are Pliocene: the Sabbie di Asti were laid down as beach sands about 5 to 3.5 million years ago.
Roero Arneis needs at least 95% Arneis and Roero rosso at least 95% Nebbiolo (art. 2).
The Roero disciplinare sets no altitude limit; it excludes north-facing slopes from -22.5 to +22.5 degrees for the reds only (art. 4).

g:IT/piemonte/asti-and-monferrato.title: Monferrato (Astigiano and Casalese)
g:IT/piemonte/asti-and-monferrato.atlas_note: The Monferrato is the broad hill country of the provinces of Asti and Alessandria between the Tanaro and the Po. In the Astigiano the soils are calcareous Miocene marls and younger Pliocene sands; around Casale older Miocene sandstones, the Pietra da Cantoni, carry the infernot cellars. The climate is temperate-continental with about 700 mm of rain. Barbera dominates, with Moscato around Canelli and Grignolino, Freisa and Ruchè as local reds.
geology: Marine sediments of the Tertiary Piedmont Basin. The Astigiano has Miocene calcareous marls (the 'terre bianche') and younger Pliocene Asti sands. In the Basso Monferrato Casalese older Miocene calcareous sandstones, the Pietra da Cantoni, rise to the surface; the infernot cellars are dug into them.
Miocene arenaceous and calcareous marls ('terre bianche') (Miocene)
The oldest soils of the Barbera d'Asti zone; mostly calcareous with much calcium carbonate (art. 9).
Sabbie astiane (Asti sands) (Pliocene)
The youngest soils of the Barbera d'Asti zone (art. 9). Nizza lies in the 'bacino pliocenico astigiano' on marly-sandstone Tertiary formations with high calcium carbonate (art. 9).
Gruppo della Pietra da Cantoni (Miocene, Burdigalian to Langhian)

Calcareous sandstones and calcareous marls, locally glauconitic with rhodolith beds, in the Basso Monferrato around Rosignano Monferrato, Cella Monte, San Giorgio Monferrato, Ozzano Monferrato, Treville and Sala Monferrato.
Pietra da Cantoni, numerical age (about 20 to 15 Ma)
Oldest part about 20 to 17.5 Ma, at Colma about 17.5 to 15 Ma. (secondary source)
Other infernot host rocks (Oligocene and Pliocene)
Some infernot are cut into the Oligocene Cardona Formation or the Pliocene Argille Azzurre and Sabbie di Asti.
Casalese soils (legal wording)

Calcareous, alkaline, rather poor soils from marine sediments; silty pale soils turn sandy and darker along an old shoreline, for example at Viarigi and Castagnole Monferrato (Grignolino del Monferrato Casalese art. 8).
climate: Temperate-continental, with cold winters of little rain (Nizza art. 9); temperate to warm temperate, about 1800 degree days (Barbera d'Asti art. 9).
700 mm rain a year. About 1800 growing degree days.
Vezzolano, Albugnano (426 m), Basso Monferrato · CNR station 1962-2004 and Regione Piemonte station 2003-2019
11.8 °C mean, 846 mm rain a year. Wettest month May (109 mm), driest January (43 mm).
The Alps (about 130 km) and the sea (about 90 km) both act on the Casalese climate; the 45th parallel crosses Vignale Monferrato (Grignolino del Monferrato Casalese art. 8).
g:IT/piemonte/asti-and-monferrato.altitude_text: Barbera d'Asti vineyards mostly 150 to 400 m (art. 9), with a limit of 650 m (art. 4). Nizza mainly 150 to 350 m, some 350 to 500 m (art. 9). Grignolino del Monferrato Casalese 120 to 350 m (art. 8).
history: A letter of 1609 in the Nizza municipal archive mentions Barbera wine tasted for the court of the Duke of Mantua (Nizza art. 9).
The Champagne method was applied to Moscato in Asti and Canelli.
Leardi and Demaria published the Ampelografia della Provincia di Alessandria, cited in the Barbera d'Asti disciplinare (art. 9).
Barbera d'Asti DOC by DPR of 9 January 1970.
Grignolino del Monferrato Casalese DOC by DPR of 26 June 1974.
Barbera d'Asti DOCG by DM of 8 July 2008.

Three UNESCO components are in the Monferrato: Nizza Monferrato and Barbera (core 2,307 ha), Canelli and Asti Spumante (1,971 ha), Monferrato of the Infernot (2,561 ha, with its own buffer zone of 16,943 ha). Nizza became a DOCG in the same year.
grapes: Barbera d'Asti needs at least 90% Barbera; Nizza is 100% Barbera. (secondary source)
The grape of Asti and Moscato d'Asti; Canelli is the UNESCO component for Asti Spumante.
Grignolino del Monferrato Casalese needs at least 95% Grignolino. (secondary source)
Ruchè di Castagnole Monferrato needs at least 90% Ruchè. (secondary source)
study_points: The Astigiano soils are Miocene 'terre bianche' (calcareous marls) and Pliocene 'sabbie astiane' (art. 9 Barbera d'Asti).
Infernot are dug in the Pietra da Cantoni, a Burdigalian to Langhian (Miocene) calcareous sandstone of the Basso Monferrato.
Barbera d'Asti vineyards are capped at 650 m (art. 4); about 700 mm of rain and 1800 degree days (art. 9).
Barbera d'Asti: DOC 1970, DOCG 2008.
The 45th parallel crosses Vignale Monferrato (Grignolino del Monferrato Casalese art. 8).

g:IT/piemonte/asti-and-monferrato.title: Gavi and Colli Tortonesi
g:IT/piemonte/asti-and-monferrato.atlas_note: Gavi and the Colli Tortonesi are in the south east of the province of Alessandria, against the Apennines and close to Liguria. The soils are marine sediments of the Tertiary Piedmont Basin, from red soils and marls at Gavi to clay-marls at Tortona. Winters are long and cold, summers cooler and windier than on the plain. Gavi makes white wine from Cortese; Tortona is the home of Timorasso.
geology: Sedimentary rocks of the Tertiary Piedmont Basin at the foot of the Ligurian Apennines. Gavi runs from red soils in the north through marl and sandstone to white clayey marls in the south. The Tortona hills are clay-marl soils on the same basin succession.
Terre rosse (Gavi)
The first of three geological bands described in the Gavi disciplinare (art. 8).
Marl and sandstone alternation (Gavi)
The central band (art. 8).
White clayey marls (Gavi)
The southern band, 'marne argillose bianche' (art. 8).
Bacino Terziario del Piemonte, clay-marl soils (Colli Tortonesi) (Tertiary)
Sedimentary terrain of the Tertiary Piedmont Basin; hills slope 15 to 30 degrees, mainly facing south west (art. 9).
Val Borbera Conglomerates (Lower Oligocene)
About 2,500 m of continental to marine conglomerates in the Borbera valley, east of Gavi. (secondary source)
climate: Transitional and moderately continental: long cold winters with frequent heavy snow; summers cooler and windier than on the nearby plain (Gavi art. 8).
Slopes steepen toward the Apennine foothills (Gavi art. 8).
history: On 3 June 972 a document now in the Archivio di Stato di Genova records a vineyard lease at Gavi (art. 8).
First reference to vineyards 'tutte di cortese' (art. 8).
Count Nuvolone's ampelography describes Cortese (art. 8).
Colli Tortonesi DOC by DPR of 9 October 1973.
Gavi DOC by DPR of 26 June 1974.
Gavi DOCG by DM of 29 July 1998.
grapes: Colli Tortonesi Timorasso needs at least 95% Timorasso (art. 2); the disciplinare calls this old, recovered grape the flag of the Colli Tortonesi (art. 9).
The Monleale sottozona of the Colli Tortonesi is for Barbera-based reds (art. 1).
study_points: Gavi has three soil bands: terre rosse, marl and sandstone, and white clayey marls (art. 8).
Cortese is named at Gavi in 1659 (art. 8).
Gavi: DOC 1974, DOCG 1998. Colli Tortonesi: DOC 1973.
Colli Tortonesi has two sottozone: Terre di Libarna (Timorasso and others) and Monleale (Barbera) (art. 1).

g:IT/piemonte/alto-piemonte.title: Alto Piemonte (Novara and Vercelli hills)
g:IT/piemonte/alto-piemonte.atlas_note: Alto Piemonte is the string of small Nebbiolo zones on the hills of Novara and Vercelli, at the foot of Monte Rosa. Their rocks are the roots of a Permian supervolcano that erupted about 280 million years ago, mixed with marine sands and glacial moraines, so soils are acid and stony. The climate is cooler and wetter than in the Langhe. Nebbiolo, called Spanna here, is blended with Vespolina and Uva Rara.
geology: The hills on both banks of the Sesia sit on the exposed plumbing of a Permian supervolcano: porphyries (volcanic rocks) and granites, with pockets of marine sand and glacial moraines from Monte Rosa. Soils are mostly acid, in contrast with the calcareous south.
Sesia supervolcano (caldera and deep magmatic system) (Permian, active 290 to 280 Ma, main eruption about 280 Ma)
Caldera at least 13 km across; the tilted crust exposes the magma chamber to about 25 to 30 km depth between Valsesia, Valsessera and Lake Maggiore. Described by Sinigoi and Quick in Geology (2009).
Volcanic subsoil with porphyry and granite (Gattinara) (Permian)
The Gattinara disciplinare (art. 9) says the subsoil is of volcanic origin, with porphyry and granite, rich in potassium, magnesium and iron.
Marine sediments on porphyry (Lessona)
Lessona is 'a tongue of marine sediments resting on deep porphyritic rock', with very acid reddish sands (art. 9).
Monte Rosa moraines (Boca, Ghemme) (Pleistocene)

Boca soils are glacial moraine from Monte Rosa with clay, sand, granite pebbles, porphyry and dolomitic fragments from Monte Fenera (art. 9). At Ghemme the Monte Rosa glaciers reached the plain and left a chain of moraines; surface layers of clay, kaolin and tuff (art. 9).
First geological map of the ten Alto Piemonte denominations
Presented in July 2026 by the Consorzio Tutela Nebbioli Alto Piemonte with Vigna Veritas. (secondary source)
climate: Sub-Alpine temperate, wetter than the southern hills.
North winds from Monte Rosa give large day-night swings at Boca; Monte Fenera shelters the zone (Boca art. 9).
At Gattinara a rocky ridge over 500 m to the east shields vineyards facing west-south-west from mountain winds (art. 9).
g:IT/piemonte/alto-piemonte.altitude_text: Gattinara 250 to 550 m, Ghemme 220 to 400 m, Boca 300 to 550 m, Lessona 200 to 500 m (art. 4 of each disciplinare). Lessona averages about 350 m (art. 9).
history: Gattinara wine was already exported (art. 9).
The State Archive of Biella records the purchase of a vineyard at Lessona (art. 9).
Mercurino di Gattinara sent barrels of local wine to European courts (art. 9).
The Regia Stazione Enologica Sperimentale was founded in Gattinara (art. 9).
Gattinara DOC by DPR of 9 July 1967.
Ghemme DOC by DPR of 18 September 1969; Boca DOC by DPR of 18 July 1969.
Gattinara DOCG by DPR of 20 October 1990.
Ghemme DOCG by DM of 29 May 1997.
grapes: Gattinara needs at least 90% Nebbiolo, Ghemme and Lessona at least 85%. (secondary source)
Blending grape of Ghemme, Boca, Fara, Sizzano and Lessona; Gattinara allows up to 4%. (secondary source)
Blending grape of the Novara and Vercelli Nebbiolo wines; Boca needs 10 to 30% Uva Rara and/or Vespolina. (secondary source)
study_points: The Sesia supervolcano erupted about 280 million years ago; its caldera was at least 13 km across.
Gattinara: volcanic subsoil with porphyry and granite (art. 9); vineyards 250 to 550 m (art. 4).
Lessona: marine sediments on deep porphyry, very acid sands (art. 9).
Gattinara DOC 1967, DOCG 1990; Ghemme DOC 1969, DOCG 1997.
The Regia Stazione Enologica Sperimentale was founded at Gattinara in 1872.

g:IT/piemonte/turin-canavese-and-pinerol.title: Canavese and Carema
g:IT/piemonte/turin-canavese-and-pinerol.atlas_note: The Canavese lies north of Turin where the Dora Baltea leaves the Aosta Valley. Its hills are the moraines of the Ivrea amphitheatre, built in about ten Pleistocene glaciations, so soils are sandy and pebbly. Caluso makes white wine, sparkling wine and passito from Erbaluce. Carema, on the Aosta Valley border, grows Nebbiolo on pergolas over dry-stone terraces.
geology: The Canavese wine hills are glacial moraines of the Ivrea morainic amphitheatre, built by the Dora Baltea glacier where it left the Aosta Valley. Carema sits on morainic rock at the Aosta Valley border, on dry-stone terraces.
Anfiteatro Morenico di Ivrea (Pleistocene, about 900,000 to 11,500 years BP; Last Glacial Maximum 29 to 19 ka cal BP)

505 km2, the third largest morainic amphitheatre of the Italian Alps, about 27 km north to south and up to 31 km wide, built in about ten glaciations. Its lateral moraine, the Serra d'Ivrea, runs about 21 km from Andrate to Dorzano.
Morainic sands and pebbles (Erbaluce di Caluso) (Pleistocene)
Sandy, pebbly soil of the Canavese morainic hills (art. 9); vineyards must be on soils of morainic origin (art. 4).
Morainic rock at Carema (Pleistocene)
Vineyards on morainic rocks at the border with the Aosta Valley, on dry-stone terraces (art. 9); soils of morainic origin (art. 4).
climate: Sub-Alpine, wetter than the southern hills.
Strong valley winds and early-autumn fog near the Aosta Valley border (Carema art. 9).
Terrace walls (topion) and stone pillars store sun heat and release it to the vines at night (Carema art. 9).
g:IT/piemonte/turin-canavese-and-pinerol.altitude_text: Erbaluce di Caluso 200 to 500 m (art. 4). Carema 300 to 600 m in art. 4, while art. 9 describes vineyards from 350 to 700 m.
history: Roman period
The Erbaluce di Caluso disciplinare states that the grape was introduced by the Romans (art. 9); this is a claim of the text, not a dated record.
Carema DOC by DPR of 9 July 1967; Erbaluce di Caluso DOC by DPR of 9 July 1967.
Erbaluce di Caluso DOCG by DM of 8 October 2010.
grapes: The white grape of Caluso; the disciplinare credits the morainic soils for the wine's base acidity and freshness (art. 9).
Carema is Nebbiolo trained on pergolas held by chestnut crossbars and stone pillars (art. 9).
study_points: The Ivrea morainic amphitheatre covers 505 km2 and is the third largest in the Italian Alps.
Erbaluce di Caluso vineyards: 200 to 500 m on morainic soils (art. 4).
Carema: pergolas on chestnut crossbars, dry-stone walls called topion (art. 9).
Carema and Erbaluce di Caluso were both DOC on 9 July 1967; Erbaluce became DOCG in 2010.

it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1235.title: Chianti Classico
it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1235.atlas_note: Chianti Classico is the historic Chianti between Florence and Siena, the zone Cosimo III bounded in 1716. Its hills are Apennine rock: galestro shale, alberese limestone and macigno and pietraforte sandstones, with the mix changing from one UGA to the next. The climate is continental, with cold winters, hot dry summers and about 800 to 900 mm of rain. Wines are at least 80% Sangiovese, and 90% for Gran Selezione.
geology: The Chianti Classico hills are Apennine rocks: galestro shales, alberese limestone, macigno and pietraforte sandstones and the Sillano formation, with Pliocene marine sands and old river deposits at the edges. Each UGA has its own mix.
Galestro (clay shale)
The disciplinare (art. 9) describes the bedrock as a shield of clay shales called galestri, with scaly clay interlayers.
Alberese (Cretaceous (flysch matrix))

Marly limestone alternating with the galestro (art. 9). CREA places it in a Cretaceous clay-marl flysch. The Consorzio says alberese and pietraforte prevail at Montefioralle; GuildSomm calls it dominant at Gaiole.
Macigno del Chianti (Oligocene)
Feldspathic sandstone of the Chianti anticline, on the high hills (CREA); non-calcareous soils, 0% CaCO3 in the sandy loam type. GuildSomm places it at Lamole, a strip of Gaiole and Vagliagli.
Pietraforte
Sandstone giving loose, stony, well-drained soils; with alberese the main formation at Montefioralle (Consorzio); also Greve, Panzano, Castellina, San Donato in Poggio (GuildSomm).
Sillano formation
Marly rock common at Greve, Castellina, San Donato in Poggio and Vagliagli. (secondary source)
Pliocene conglomerates and marine sands; fluvial deposits (Pliocene and later)
On low and medium hills at the edges of the zone (CREA landscapes 5, 8 and 9); old reddish river deposits at San Casciano (GuildSomm).
climate: Continental (art. 9): winters below 4 to 5 C, dry hot summers often above 35 C.
850 mm rain a year. Given as 'about 800 to 900 mm', mostly in late autumn and spring; 850 is the midpoint.
The Monti del Chianti on the east side and the Apennines to the north east. Lamole has the highest vineyards, above 700 m; Radda is more than 75% forest, which helps night cooling. (secondary source)
it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1235.altitude_text: Vineyards may not be above 700 m (art. 4). The disciplinare puts the base near 200 m and the median elevation no higher than about 600 m (art. 9). UGA ranges run from 110 m (San Casciano, Greve) to 715 m (Lamole).
history: First notarial deed using the name Chianti for the wine of this area (art. 9).
Cosimo III defined the Chianti zone, called by the disciplinare the first wine zone in the world defined by law (art. 9).
On 14 May 1924, 33 producers founded the consorzio for the defence of Chianti wine (art. 9).
An interministerial decree allowed the historic zone to use 'Classico' (art. 9).
DOC by DPR of 9 August 1967.
DOCG by DPR of 2 July 1984.
Own disciplinare, separate from Chianti, by decree of 5 August 1996.
The amendment of DM 22 June 2023 (GU 1 July 2023) brought in 11 UGA for Gran Selezione labels.
grapes: 80 to 100% for Chianti Classico and Riserva; 90 to 100% for Gran Selezione (art. 2).
Native reds allowed in Gran Selezione within the 10% left after Sangiovese (art. 2).
study_points: Vineyards above 700 m are excluded (art. 4).
Galestro and alberese are named in the disciplinare (art. 9); macigno is Oligocene sandstone (CREA).
There are 11 UGA, used only on Gran Selezione.
Chianti Classico: DOC 1967, DOCG 1984, separate from Chianti in 1996.
Sangiovese: minimum 80%, Gran Selezione minimum 90% (art. 2).

it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1228.title: Chianti (outer zones)
it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1228.atlas_note: Chianti DOCG is the large zone around Chianti Classico, on hills of six provinces. Its sottozone go from the Colline Pisane in the west to the Colli Aretini in the east and the Colli Senesi in the south. The climate gives about 867 mm of rain a year, and vineyards lie mostly between 200 and 400 m. The wines are Sangiovese-based.
geology: The Chianti DOCG wraps around Chianti Classico across the provinces of Arezzo, Florence, Pisa, Pistoia, Prato and Siena. The disciplinare calls it geologically homogeneous, south of the Apennines, with soils from clay to sand.
Clay to sandy soils (legal wording)
A geologically homogeneous zone south of the Apennines; soils range from clay to sandy, including clay with stones, of medium fertility (art. 9).
climate: Hill climate with cool winters and warm summers (art. 9).
867 mm rain a year. Range 817 to 932 mm; wettest month November (121 mm), driest July (32 mm); August averages over 23 C and January about 5 C.
it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1228.altitude_text: Hill vineyards mostly between 200 and 400 m (art. 9).
history: Grand Ducal rules of September 1716 set the terms for trade in Chianti wine (art. 9).
DM of 31 July 1932 first delimited the zone and its zones Montalbano, Rufina, Colli Fiorentini and Colli Senesi (art. 3 and art. 9).
DOC by DPR of 9 August 1967.
DOCG by DPR of 2 July 1984.
Montespertoli added as a sottozona by decree of 8 September 1997 (art. 3).
grapes: Up to 15% in Chianti, 10% in Colli Senesi; white grapes up to 10%. (secondary source)
study_points: Average rainfall 867 mm (817 to 932); November wettest, July driest (art. 9).
The Chianti zone was first delimited by DM of 31 July 1932 (art. 9).
Chianti: DOC 1967, DOCG 1984.
Sottozone in art. 1: Colli Aretini, Colli Fiorentini, Colli Senesi, Colline Pisane, Montalbano, Montespertoli, Rufina, plus the newer Terre di Vinci.

it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1199.title: Montalcino
it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1199.atlas_note: Montalcino is a single hill commune south of Siena, between the Orcia and Ombrone valleys. Its soils are mixed, from loose clay and sand low down to stony marl and limestone near the top. The climate is dry and Mediterranean, with about 700 mm of rain, sheltered by Monte Amiata to the south. Brunello, 100% Sangiovese, was DOC in 1966 and DOCG in 1980.
geology: The hill of Montalcino formed over several geological eras and has many soil types (art. 9). Low ground has looser soils; higher up, stony soils from marl and limestone. Producers describe clay low in the west turning sandy higher up with galestro at the top, and river deposits low in the north and east.
Mixed soils of several eras (legal wording)
Many soil environments; vineyard soils poor in organic matter and calcareous (art. 9).
Loose soils low, stony marl and limestone soils high
Lowest areas have relatively loose soils; higher up the soil is dense with stones from the breakdown of marl and limestone.
Clay, sand and galestro by height; fluvial deposits north and east
Lowest western parts mostly clay subsoils, sandy higher up, galestro at the top; in the east and north the lowest zones are mainly river deposits. (secondary source)
climate: Mediterranean, mostly dry, with occasional continental spells (art. 9 and Consorzio).
700 mm rain a year. Mostly in spring and late autumn.
Mount Amiata (1,740 m) to the south shelters the zone from storms.
Montalcino is 40 km from the sea and 100 km from the Apennines.
The north is the coolest part and Torrenieri is rainy; the tramontana hits the north and east, the scirocco the hilltops and west. (secondary source)
it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1199.altitude_text: From about 120 m along the rivers to about 650 m near Poggio Civitella (art. 9; Consorzio).
history: Clemente Santi, the founding father of Brunello, won a silver medal for his 1865 vintage.
Brunello di Montalcino DOC by DPR of 28 March 1966.
The Consorzio del Vino Brunello di Montalcino was founded.
DOCG by DPR of 1 July 1980; the Consorzio calls it the first wine to become DOCG.
grapes: Brunello and Rosso di Montalcino are 100% Sangiovese.
Grown for Moscadello di Montalcino DOC, 50 ha.
study_points: Vineyards run from about 120 to 650 m (art. 9).
About 700 mm of rain a year; Monte Amiata (1,740 m) shelters the zone; 40 km from the sea.
Of about 4,400 ha under vine, 2,100 ha are Brunello DOCG and 860 ha Rosso di Montalcino DOC.
Brunello: DOC 1966, DOCG 1980, the first DOCG according to the Consorzio.

it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1308.title: Montepulciano
it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1308.atlas_note: Montepulciano is a hill town south east of Siena, above the Val di Chiana. Its vineyards, 250 to 600 m up, grow on Pliocene marine sands and clays. The climate is Mediterranean with about 690 mm of rain. Vino Nobile is at least 70% Sangiovese, locally called Prugnolo gentile, and since 2025 the best sites can carry one of 12 Pieve names.
geology: Marine Pliocene sands and clays on the ridge between the Val di Chiana and the Val d'Orcia; sands dominate at the higher altitudes (art. 9).
Pliocene marine sands and clays (Pliocene)
Substrate mostly of marine Pliocene sediments; sands predominate, especially higher up (art. 9).
climate: Mediterranean, hottest in July and August (art. 9).
690 mm rain a year. About 740 mm in the south of the zone. Winkler index about 1900, 1750 at the highest sites.
it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1308.altitude_text: Vineyards between 250 and 600 m (art. 4.1 and art. 9).
history: Earliest document: a cleric offers vineyard land to the church of San Silvestro sull'Amiata (art. 9).
A document sets the first clauses for the trade and export of the wine (art. 9).
mid-16th century
Sante Lancerio, cellarer of Pope Paul III Farnese, praised the wine (art. 9).
Francesco Redi's 'Bacco in Toscana' (art. 9).
DOC by DPR of 12 July 1966.
DOCG by DPR of 1 July 1980.
DM of 21 January 2025 (GU 5 February 2025) added 12 UGA that follow the word 'Pieve'.
grapes: At least 70% in Vino Nobile; at least 85% for the Pieve wines (art. 2).
The only grapes allowed with Sangiovese in the Pieve wines, up to 15%, Colorino at most 5% (art. 2).
study_points: Vineyards 250 to 600 m (art. 4.1).
Soils: marine Pliocene sands and clays, sandier higher up (art. 9).
Twelve Pievi (UGA) since the DM of 21 January 2025; Pieve wines need 85% Sangiovese.
Vino Nobile: DOC 1966, DOCG 1980.

it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1292.title: San Gimignano
it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1292.atlas_note: San Gimignano is the towered hill town west of Siena. Its vineyards, 70 to 500 m up, grow on Pliocene sea floor of yellow sands and clays. The climate is sub-Mediterranean with about 700 mm of rain. The white Vernaccia di San Gimignano was the first Italian DOC in 1966.
geology: Soils formed on marine Pliocene deposits: yellow sands (locally called tufo) and yellow and grey clays (art. 9).
Pliocene marine sands and clays (Pliocene)
Yellow sands ('tufo') and yellow and grey clays (art. 9).
climate: Sub-Mediterranean, with dry summers and rather cold winters (art. 9).
it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1292.altitude_text: Vineyards between 70 and 500 m; the production territory runs from 67 to 629 m (art. 9).

it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1348.title: Bolgheri and the Etruscan coast
it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1348.atlas_note: Bolgheri is the coastal amphitheatre of the commune of Castagneto Carducci, between the Tyrrhenian Sea and the Colline Metallifere. Its soils are young marine and alluvial deposits, gravels and sands that change over short distances. The climate is Mediterranean, dry and windy, with about 600 mm of rain. Bordeaux varieties dominate, led by Cabernet Sauvignon since the first Sassicaia vines of 1944.
geology: A coastal strip of marine and alluvial deposits below the Colline Metallifere. Streams from the hills built gravelly fans and terraces over older Pleistocene marine sands; soils run from sand to clay over short distances.
Conglomerati di Bolgheri (Middle Pleistocene)
Named by Mazzanti (1983); used as the reference for similar Middle Pleistocene conglomerates on the Grosseto coast.
Sabbie di Donoratico (Upper Pleistocene)
Coastal sands of the Castagneto area, cited as a reference unit.
Marine and alluvial soils (Consorzio zoning)
Marine and alluvial origin. The zoning led by Attilio Scienza, completed in 2006, found 27 soil units, mostly sandy clay loam, alkaline and deep with fine gravel and sometimes fossil shells.
Heterogeneous textures (legal wording)
Soils vary from sandy and sandy-clay-loam to clay or silty clay (art. 9).
Dunes, terraces and ridges
An earlier zoning separated a sandy dune zone, a terrace zone (Castagneto, Contessine) and ridges (Segalari, Colle Rosi).
climate: 14.5 °C mean, 584 mm rain a year. Mean minimum 9.6 C, mean maximum 19.4 C, water deficit 205 mm.

g:IT/toscana/maremma-and-the-coast.title: Maremma (Scansano, Montecucco)
g:IT/toscana/maremma-and-the-coast.atlas_note: The Maremma is southern Tuscany, from the coast near Grosseto inland to Monte Amiata. Scansano sits on sandstone and limestone hills with shallow soils; Montecucco lies on mixed sediments at the foot of Amiata. The climate is Mediterranean and dry, about 14 to 15 C and 620 to 800 mm of rain. Sangiovese, called Morellino at Scansano, is the main grape.
geology: Inland Maremma hills of sandstone, limestone and clay-schist. At Scansano sandstone ridges lie to the west and calcareous rocks to the east; Montecucco mixes Neogene and Quaternary sediments over older tectonic units at the foot of Monte Amiata.
Macigno and pietraforte sandstone ridges (west Scansano)
Western sector sandstone ridges of macigno and pietraforte type; loam-silt or sandy-loam soils (art. 10).
Calcareous and clay-schist formations (east Scansano)
Eastern sector; clay-loam or silty-loam soils; soils generally shallow with bedrock near the surface (art. 10).
Neogene and Quaternary sediments on tectonic units (Montecucco) (Neogene to Quaternary)
Varied lithology with Plio-Quaternary fluvio-lacustrine deposits; soils mostly from sandstones, on marly and pelitic hills, loamy and stony (art. 9).
climate: 15.0 °C mean, 620 mm rain a year. About 7 C in winter and 24 C in summer; rain mostly November to April; drought is the main limit (art. 10).
14.25 °C mean, 775 mm rain a year. Given as 14 to 14.5 C and 750 to 800 mm (midpoints shown); July minimum 19.5 mm, November maximum 115 mm; Huglin index 2300 to 2500 (art. 9).
Montecucco runs from the slopes of Monte Amiata toward Grosseto (art. 9).
g:IT/toscana/maremma-and-the-coast.altitude_text: Scansano: mean 250 m, down to 30 to 40 m in low areas, maximum 566 m (art. 10). Montecucco: vineyards about 120 to 500 m, area mean about 200 m (art. 9).
history: Etruscan period
Vine growing at Scansano dates to the Etruscans, with evidence from Ghiaccioforte (art. 10); at Montecucco finds near Seggiano and Potentino (art. 9).
First detailed production records: 5,540 hl of wine in the Scansano area (art. 10).

it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1220.title: Carmignano
it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1220.atlas_note: Carmignano lies on the south-west slopes of the Montalbano, west of Florence, in the communes of Carmignano and Poggio a Caiano. Its soils are macigno sandstone with clay schist and marl on top. Vineyards stay below 400 m, with less than 1,000 mm of rain. Carmignano was named in the 1716 Medici edict, and its rules require 10 to 20% Cabernet with Sangiovese.
geology: The Montalbano ridge west of Florence: a core of macigno sandstone overlain by clay schists and calcareous marl (art. 9).
Macigno core (Oligocene (age from CREA for the Chianti macigno))
Light sandy-loam soils on the sandstone (art. 9).
Clay schists and calcareous marl

climate: Hill climate with a good day-night range from cool night winds (art. 9).
Average rainfall is under 1,000 mm a year (art. 9).
it-eupdo-PDO-IT-A1220.altitude_text: Vineyards may not be above 400 m (art. 4.2); the sunny slopes rarely exceed 300 m, the plain is at 40 to 50 m and the top is Poggio al Ciliegio at 611 m (art. 9).

it-deep-chianti-rufina.title: Rufina
it-deep-chianti-rufina.atlas_note: Rufina is one of the old Chianti zones, in the Sieve valley north east of Florence at the foot of the Apennines. Its higher part, Pomino, reaches 750 m and has grown French varieties since 1855. The climate has hot summers, cold winters and wide temperature swings. Chianti Rufina is a Sangiovese-based sottozona of Chianti, delimited in 1932.
geology: Hills of the Sieve valley at the foot of the Apennines. The only official soil text found is for Pomino, inside the Rufina area: mainly sandstone and marl soils, siliceous and micaceous, with little clay.
Sandstone and marl soils (Pomino)
Mainly arenaceous and marly, with prevailing siliceous and micaceous content and little clay (Pomino art. 9).
climate: Strong temperature swings, hot summers and harsh winters (Pomino art. 9).
550 to 700 mm depending on the year (art. 9).
Chianti Rufina lies in the Val di Sieve, 20 km north east of Florence.
it-deep-chianti-rufina.altitude_text: Pomino vineyards lie between 300 and 750 m (art. 9); new plantings no higher than 650 m for red and 800 m for white (art. 4.1). No official altitude range was found for Chianti Rufina itself.
history: The bando of 24 September 1716 protected the name 'Pomino', which then covered both the Pomino and Rufina areas. (secondary source)
Vittorio degli Albizi introduced French varieties at Pomino, among them Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and Blanc, Chardonnay and Sauvignon (Pomino art. 9).
Rufina was one of the zones delimited by the DM of 31 July 1932.

grapes: Base of Chianti Rufina, a sottozona of the Chianti DOCG (art. 1.1).
